refuted_findings.title: Game-night executor latency contaminates the week-1 measurement (B, labelled)
refuted_findings.claim: The executor's 15 s period, EXEC_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS 10 s and the fix-26 batch floor of 250 rows are sized to the NAS; on the one-game Thursday the loop ran avg 27.5 s / p95 115-118 s in the 19:00 hour (5-6x the period), p95 exceeded the 7.5 s ceiling on 3 of 4 days, 521 of 17,138 loops were skipped (3.0 %), and orders were placed with staleness_at_place p50 67 s / p95 94 s of a 220 s allowance, so cancel and placement decisions ran up to 2 min late and order lifetimes were compressed. Saturday/Sunday slates are larger than what broke the box on Thursday.
reasons: evidence: Citation audit. VERIFIED: harness/db/engine.py:6 EXEC_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000 (comment: sized to the loop period, 'a query that outlives the loop period is a stall'); harness/config/settings.py:54 exec_period_s = 15; harness/execution/store.py:493 DELTA_BATCH_FLOOR = 250 with the comment at 484-492 'a measurement, not a guess: on the NAS under I/O pressure' (cited range is the comment, constant is line 493); docs/superpowers/autopilot/verify.md:117 loop-metrics row 'p95_loop_ms under exec_period_s x 1000 / 2' = 7.5 s; evidence.md D2 rows 18:00 avg 18,286 p95 101,062 / 19:00 avg 27,533 p95 114,768 / 20:00 p95 72,603 max 256,171 exact; evidence D1 daily p95 16,205 / 6,188 / 15,169 / 10,033 ms => 3 of 4 days over 7.5 s (09-11 is partial to 07:30 and includes the deploy storm and pg_dump window, not game load); evidence.md line 460 exec_heartbeat loops 17,138 loops_skipped 521 = 3.04 % (loop.py:1213-1219: skipped = whole periods missed between consecutive loop starts, cumulative since the counter started, all causes: deploy storms at 03:16-03:18 added 431->443 per journal 109, swap-back added +70 per journal 107); evidence G stale_p50 67 / p95 94 / allow 220 on n=7,825 exact; journal 101 '19:00 avg 27.5 s p95 118 s', loops_skipped 354 at 20:07; journal 107 half-hour p95 9.1-15.2 s 'still over the 7.5 s p95 ceiling'; journal 109 loops 336 s at 03:31 and 235 s at 03:37 in the pg_dump + RFQ replay window. MISREAD (load-bearing): the G staleness_at_place citation. harness/execution/plan.py:194-197 says explicitly that staleness_s and stale_allowance_s are 'the signal's gap-snapshot values -- pricing-time quantities, carried through to the order and never recomputed at the loop clock'; loop.py:1037 copies market.staleness_s into staleness_at_place; harness/pricing/fair.py:130-133 defines it as now - newest_book_ts at pricing time (age of the sharp-book quote when the fair was computed), and the 220 s allowance is FEATURED_CADENCE_S 120 + tick_budget_s 100 (fair.py:24,30-35), a pricing-tick budget. So p50 67 s / p95 94 s measures Odds API quote age at pricing, not executor lag, and cannot support 'placement decisions ran up to 2 min late'. Evidence G by-day confirms it is uncorrelated with loop latency: avg_stale 65/68/71/56 s on days whose loop p95 was 16.2/6.2/15.2/10.0 s. CONTRADICTED: 'order lifetimes were compressed' -- evidence G by-day time-in-book p50 was 15.5 min on 09-10 (the bad day) vs 12.2 on 09-09 and 4.8 on 09-08; the game-night hour subset is unverified but the cited table shows longer, not shorter, lifetimes. OVERSTATED/MISLABELLED: '5-6x the period' -- journal 101's 'five to six times' is wall clock vs the normal ~5 s loop; against the 15 s period the 19:00 avg is 1.8x and the p95 7.9x. 'one-game Thursday' -- journal 101 records two games in progress (LAR-SF game 2 and game 371). 'up to 2 min late' understates the cited data: 19:00 max 163 s, 20:00 max 256 s. UNVERIFIED EXTRAPOLATION: 'Saturday/Sunday slates are larger than what broke the box' -- journal 101 attributes the Thursday failure to NAS memory (swap 5,021 MB resident, memory pressure full 16 %, media stack ~1.3 GiB) with the executor's own work flat (dirty_markets 107-117, intents 500-1,260, 'same work, five to six times the wall clock'); that cause was removed at 20:12 (journal 102) and loops recovered to avg 7-9 s (journal 107). No cited number links executor load to number of live games; evidence note 9 shows 92 % of orders are placed >24 h before kickoff. The latency facts stand, but the causal chain from latency to contaminated orders rests on a misread column and a contradicted sub-claim, so the finding as written is refuted; a narrower version survives.

alternative: The latency numbers are real (evidence D2; journal 101/107) but the causal chain and the "contaminates the week-1 measurement" conclusion rest on four misreadings, each better supported the other way.

(1) staleness_at_place is not executor latency. harness/pricing/fair.py:130-133 `_staleness_s(now, newest_ts)` = seconds between the PRICING tick and the sharp book's newest `last_update`; harness/execution/plan.py:194-197: "`staleness_s` and `stale_allowance_s` are the signal's gap-snapshot values -- pricing-time quantities, carried through to the order and never recomputed at the loop clock"; loop.py:1036-1037 just copies them; the 220 s allowance = FEATURED_CADENCE_S 120 + tick_budget_s 100 (fair.py:24,30-35). So G's p50 67 s / p95 94 s measures Odds API featured-feed lag, and the inference "so cancel and placement decisions ran up to 2 min late" does not follow from that column.

(2) "Order lifetimes were compressed" is contradicted by evidence G by day: 09-10 (the game night) has the LONGEST fair_stale time-in-book of the four days (p25 5.5 / p50 15.5 / p75 36.8 min vs 09-09 1.5 / 12.2 / 33.7; 09-08 1.3 / 4.8 / 62). In the slow hours D4 shows placed/cancelled 285/167 (20:00), 10/10 (21:00), 9/9 (22:00) with open_orders pinned at 150.0 (D3) — no cancel wave; the fast 17:00 hour (p95 12.5 s) had the most churn (441/591). The fair_stale rule does run at loop clock (plan.py:452-456, loop.py:108), so a >100 s loop on top of the ~2 min fair refresh (evidence F) CAN cause a spurious cancel, but the data show it did not materially on 09-10.

(3) Cause on Thursday was host memory, not executor sizing or slate size. Journal 101: "NAS memory FAIL (the cause)": swap 5,021 MB resident, swap-in/out 382/1822 per 5 s, memory pressure full avg300 16 %, media stack ~1.3 GiB; "the executor's own work is flat: dirty_markets 107-117, intents_considered 500-1,260 ... same work, five to six times the wall clock". Journal 102: media stopped 20:12 CT; journal 107: p95 back to 9.1-15.2 s by 21:30-23:00, pressure full avg300 0.89 %. The executor's per-loop work is bounded by exec_max_open_orders 150 (settings.py:64) and ws_max_tickers 500 (settings.py:21), so it does not grow with the Saturday slate; what scales with the slate is app-run pricing/signals and tape volume (a different finding). Of the three "sized to the NAS" constants only DELTA_BATCH_FLOOR 250 is a NAS measurement (store.py:485-492); EXEC_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS is a fail-fast rule with no NAS rationale (engine.py:4-6) and exec_period_s 15 carries none (settings.py:54).

(4) "p95 over the ceiling on 3 of 4 days" conflates causes: 09-08 p95 16.2 s is the fix-22 unindexed delta-read storm (journal 68 at journal.md:955, loops 30-140 s, fixed by fixes 22/26, p95 4.3 s and 2.9 s afterwards at journal.md:1003,1039); 09-11 p95 10.0 s (364 samples to 07:30) is the phase 5 deploy storm + nightly dump + RFQ replay (journal 109/110). Only 09-10 is a game-night datum; 09-09, a full day at the 150 cap for 15 hours (D3) with no deploy storm, passed at 6.19 s. Likewise loops_skipped 521 is a counter spanning restarts (journal.md:1111): 162 on 09-09 14:35 CT (entry 86), 354 at 20:07 09-10 (journal 101, after two 09-10 morning deploys, entries 95/98), 424 at 23:17 (+70 swap-back), 521 by 07:30 09-11 (+97 in the deploy/dump/RFQ storms) — game night accounts for at most half. Also exec.loop_ms is one length-biased sample per metric_sample_s 60 s (settings.py:93; loop.py:171-175 writes the duration of whichever loop was running when the sampler came due), so an hourly p95 over samples overstates the true p95: the executor's own rolling p95 over the last 100 loops (DURATION_WINDOW loop.py:106) was 42,128 ms at 20:07 (journal 101) against the sample-derived 114,768 ms.

On contamination of the measurement: the gate quantity is queue_model fills (R12, adversarial review F). 92 % of orders were placed >24 h before kickoff and only 47 NFL orders were within 6 h of kickoff in four days (evidence note 9, G by ttk); a 100 s late loop on a market 24-72 h out with 8-15k contracts queued ahead (G per-variant) does not change whether it fills. Zero queue_model fills since 09-08 10:00 CT on every day including 09-09 at p95 6.2 s (evidence note 5), so the week-1 result is the same on the fast day as on the slow one. Whether a Saturday slate breaks the box is unverified in both directions (no executor has run through a Saturday; phase 3 deployed 09-08).

refuted_findings.title: WS sink statement timeouts discard tape and dirty books on game nights (B, labelled)
refuted_findings.claim: The WebSocket sink runs on the default 30 s statement-timeout engine; under NAS I/O pressure a timed-out commit rolls back up to commit_every=100 events and writes gap rows that dirty every affected book until a clean snapshot re-anchors it. Counts: 7 disconnects in 5 min during the 4.5 deploy storm, 40 in 7 h overnight 09-10, 33 in 3 h and 50 in 3 h during LAR-SF. The discarded-event total and the game-night gap-row count are unverified (ws.gaps was 0 over the last 6 quiet hours).
reasons: evidence: Two load-bearing citations are misread. (1) Mechanism: a timed-out commit is caught in WsSink._maybe_commit (harness/recorder/ws_sink.py:62-71): log, rollback, counters reset, NO gap rows. The cited sink_exception gap-row path (:171-214) is reached only by an exception inside handle()'s try block (:106-170), whose only SQL statement is the trade INSERT at :131; snapshot/delta frames are session.add only, so a statement timeout on them can land only at commit, which discards silently and leaves books clean-but-wrong (the case the comment at :178-180 warns about), not dirty. Trades are ~1% of frames (evidence J: ws.trades_per_min 19.6 vs ws.events_per_min 1,933). (2) Attribution: ws_disconnect rows are written only from WsRecorder.run_forever's outer except (harness/venues/kalshi/ws.py:373-387); sink.handle (ws_sink.py:171) and _maybe_commit (:66) swallow their exceptions and cannot reach it. The only unguarded DB calls in the recv loop are select_ws_tickers (ws.py:321-323 every 300 s; :333-335 at connect) on the same default 30 s engine, so a QueryCanceled ws_disconnect is the ticker-selection query timing out, not the sink's insert or commit. Journal line 368 (2026-09-07) shows exactly this path: 'ws loop error: OperationalError(QueryCanceled: statement timeout); reconnecting in 1s', reconnected 18 s later with 96 fresh snapshots and 0 gap rows. On that path the pending batch is flushed (ws.py:367-372), not discarded. Journal 90/92's 'statement timeouts in the WS sink' is the journal author's attribution, not code-verified; journal 101/107 record no reason ('WebSocket churn'). This code shape predates every cited date (replan loop 7b27916 2026-09-06; sink swallow fa806c3 2026-09-06; marks 9fcb5e0 2026-09-07). (3) Gap rows: no journal entry records a nonzero tape gap-row count (zeros at journal lines 86, 100, 126, 165, 191, 218 'raw.exposed_by read: no rows at all', 287, 367, 368, 449, 586, 629, 643 '0 today over 10,153,098 events', 941, 1312, 1317); ws.gaps 0 over 6 h (evidence J). The disconnect counts (7/40/33/50) are verified literally against journal 90/92/101/107, and engine.py:11 + cli.py:814 (default 30 s engine) and ws_sink.py:31 (commit_every=100) are correct, but they do not support the stated rollback-to-gap-rows-to-dirty-books chain. A real, smaller finding survives: the recorder's own 300 s select_ws_tickers replan on the 30 s default engine drops the socket on every timeout, and tape lost during a reconnect window is unmarked by gap rows (journal line 81 of the drill report: 'no gap rows can mark it (the socket was closed)').

alternative: The claim ties three things together that the code separates: (1) the sink's 30 s engine, (2) commit rollbacks that write gap rows, and (3) the ws_disconnect counts as the measure of (2). Two of the three links fail on the code. LINK 2 (commit -> gap rows) is wrong: a timed-out commit is caught inside `_maybe_commit` (harness/recorder/ws_sink.py:62-71; unchanged since fa806c3, 2026-09-06), which logs, rolls back, bumps `self.errors` and writes NO mark. The `exposed_by="sink_exception"` gap rows (:194-207) are written only by `handle()`'s `except` at :171, whose `try` (:106-170) contains no commit; the only DB statement that executes inside it is the immediate trade insert at :131 (plus SQLAlchemy autoflush of pending delta/snapshot rows on that execute). So the reviewer's "timed-out commit ... writes gap rows" path does not exist; the commit path is a silent hole, which journal 16 ruling (2) explicitly accepted as "phase 3 Task 3b's ... silent discard when the database itself fails". LINK 3 (disconnect counts measure sink discards) is wrong: nothing in the sink can raise into the recorder loop -- `handle` swallows (:171-214, including a second guard at :209-213), `_maybe_commit` swallows (:64-69), and every `flush`/`write_event`/`write_metrics` call in harness/venues/kalshi/ws.py is wrapped (:293-296, :342-345, :369-372, :382-387, :266-271). A `ws_disconnect` row is written only from `run_forever`'s except at ws.py:373-384, which is reachable by `_Reconnect` (no ack in 15 s :285-286, silence >= ws_stale_s 180 s :287-288, gap recovery failed twice :219, subscription rejected :319-320), by socket errors, and by the one un-guarded DB statement in the loop: `select_ws_tickers` (ws.py:322-324 every 300 s, and :334-335 on every connect attempt), which runs on the recorder's own `self.factory()` session on the same default 30 s engine (cli.py:814). The only logged disconnect reason in the repo (docs/superpowers/autopilot/evidence/2026-09-07-verify-1542-layer2.txt:88 `ws loop error: OperationalError(QueryCanceled ...)`) is therefore a ticker-selection query timeout, not a sink insert -- journal 28 anomaly (1) and journals 90/92/93 mis-attribute it to "the sink's insert" / "statement timeouts in the WS sink", contradicting the catch-all at ws_sink.py:171. The 40-vs-23 (journal 92) and 50-vs-21 (journal 107) disconnect/connect disparities (17 and 29 failed reconnect attempts) fit the `select_ws_tickers` call at ws.py:334 failing again on the cold reconnect, which the sink path cannot produce at all. The consequence of this real mechanism is benign for books: the pending batch is committed on the way out (`finally: self.sink.flush()` ws.py:365-372, commit 2601e75), sequences are reset (:355), and the venue re-sends a snapshot for every ticker on the new subscription -- journal 28: "reconnected at 20:46:36Z with 96 fresh snapshots and 0 gap rows"; the loss is a tape hole per episode (18 s there; up to the 60 s backoff cap ws.py:388 when reconnects fail) during which the executor serves the book as stale-by-age (exec_book_max_age_s 120, plan.py:246-256), not dirty. Also: fix 32 (roadmap line 352, journal 93) named BRIN autosummarize the cause of "the WS sink timeouts (40 disconnects in 7 h)", yet 33 and 50 disconnects followed on 09-10 evening after fix 32 was deployed 07:13 CT, under swap/IO pressure (journal 101), which points to the memory-bound query, not the sink. What survives: cli.py:814 does use the default engine; `_maybe_commit` silently discards up to commit_every=100 rows on a commit timeout with no mark and no exported metric (`self.errors` is never sampled; `_write_ws_metrics` ws.py:254-264 exports events/trades/subscribed/reconnects/gaps/sink_lag only); and a trade-frame timeout at :131 does write sink_exception marks that dirty every pending sid (book.py:93) with no resubscribe queued (the except path at :171-214 never touches `gap_sids`, unlike `_check_seq` :98), so such a book stays dirty until the next reconnect or 300 s re-plan adds/removes its ticker. The frequency of either sink path is unverified: no journal entry, evidence file, or metric records a `sink_exception` row or a sink commit failure in production; the ws.gaps metric (which counts the marks, ws_sink.py:207) was 0 over the last 6 h per the reviewer's evidence J, and evidence.md itself was not present at review time.

materiality: Mechanism is real but the finding is mis-described and mis-prioritised for the owner's 1-2 week decisions. (1) Wrong path: a timed-out COMMIT is caught in `_maybe_commit` (harness/recorder/ws_sink.py:62-71), rolled back and NOT marked: no gap row, no dirty book, silent hole. The `exposed_by=sink_exception` marks (ws_sink.py:194-205) are written only when a statement inside `handle` fails, and the only real statement there is the venue_trades insert (ws_sink.py:~122). (2) Sink exceptions never raise out of `handle`, so they do not produce `ws_disconnect`; those events come from unguarded DB calls in the recorder loop, chiefly `select_ws_tickers` at connect (harness/venues/kalshi/ws.py:334) and at the 300 s replan (ws.py:322-326). Disconnects exceeding connects (40/23 journal 92, 50/21 journal 107) means roughly 40 % were failed connect attempts with no socket to lose, so the disconnect counts are not a proxy for discarded tape. (3) Bounded recovery: every reconnect resubscribes and receives fresh snapshots that re-anchor books (journal 28 addendum: reconnect after a QueryCanceled, 96 fresh snapshots, 0 gap rows, 18 s hole); backoff 1 s doubling to a 60 s cap (ws.py:389). (4) Dirty books are dominated by the 120 s age rule, not sink gaps: exec.dirty_markets avg 122.8 / heartbeat book_dirty_markets 125 while ws.gaps = 0 over 6 quiet hours (evidence.md D5/D6 and J; spec phase3 design line 33 makes age > exec_book_max_age_s dirty). Attribution unverified but the sink cannot explain 125 dirty markets with zero gaps. (5) The gate already screens it (harness/report/gate.py:124,274: 80 % with book_source=ws and dirty_minutes=0) and the gate is 149 fill events short of the 150 threshold (brief: 1 queue_model order in 3 days); viability turns on fair_stale churn (7,825 cancels), not tape gaps. (6) The Mac mini trigger was already met on swap (journal 101); this is another symptom of the same I/O pressure, additive not decision-changing. "Disappears on an SSD host" is unverified: journal 93 attributed the sink timeouts to unsummarized BRIN (fixed 07:13 CT 09-10, journal 96 saw none afterward), yet 33 and 50 disconnects followed that evening under swap thrash. Discarded-event total and game-night gap-row count remain unverified. Net: nothing the owner does this week changes because of it.

refuted_findings.title: 483 intents in 24 h reached neither an order nor a skip row (B, silent at the row level)
refuted_findings.claim: intents_without_order_or_skip fails at 483 (threshold 0) at 04:15 CT; load_intents reads only intents inside exec_intent_ttl_s = 900 (`lower` = now - ttl) and an intent that ages out unconsidered writes no skip event, so executor latency or downtime loses intents silently; the 24 h window covers the LAR-SF thrash and the 03:15-03:45 deploy/dump storm (one loop in ten minutes at 03:41). 483 is ~1.6 % of a day's ~29k intents; the mechanism is inferred, not verified.
reasons: alternative: The count is real (evidence.md §I: 483 at 2026-09-11 09:15:53Z; journal 92: 0 at the 2026-09-10 04:25 CT run), but the claimed mechanism is structurally impossible and the storm attribution is contradicted by the record. (1) Intents are created by the executor itself, not by pricing: harness/execution/loop.py:406-411 computes lower = now - intent_ttl_s, calls store.candidate_signals -> store.insert_intents (created_at = the loop's `now`, store.py insert_intents) -> store.load_intents, all in one transaction, and _CANDIDATES and _NEWEST_INTENTS apply the same `signal_created_at >= :lower` bound. An intent is always read back in the loop that wrote it; the TTL drops *signals* older than 900 s (no row anywhere, invisible to this check), never intents. (2) The 03:15-03:45 deploy/dump storm cannot be in the 483: the last intent was 00:51 CT (brief) and journal 109 states "no new intents inside the window, the executor placed nothing at 03:00"; the 05:20-05:24 executor outage (journal 110) is after the 04:15 check; no gap over 900 s is evidenced in the window (evidence D: exec.loops_skipped max 24 = 6 min; D1 max loop 256 s on 09-10). (3) Two code-certain paths leave an intent with neither an order nor a `skipped` row and are not excused by the check: (A) superseded siblings: _CANDIDATES has no per-key dedup and insert_intents writes one intent per signal, but _NEWEST_INTENTS (`distinct on (variant_id, venue_market_id, side)`) and plan.py:431 _newest_by_key pass only the newest per key to plan_actions, so an older sibling gets no action whenever two pricing signals on one key land between consecutive loops; pricing runs every 1-3.5 min (evidence.md contradiction 1) while 09-10 18:00-21:00 CT loops ran p95 101-115 s, max 256 s (evidence D2). Journal 79 already recorded this exact shape on 09-09 ("2,452 were then superseded by the next pricing run's intent") and the phase 4.5 correction (checks.py:190-217, spec ruling B-(c)) excused only the subset with a working order on the key. (B) blocking cap gates: plan.py:546-550 emits CapGate and returns without a Skip when apply_caps is true; loop.py writes it as kind="cap_gate", a kind distinct from "skipped" by design (phase 3 spec line 73); the check tests only kind = 'skipped' and `cap_gate` appears nowhere in checks.py, tests/test_checks.py, verify.md or roadmap.md. Only `constrained` has apply_caps: true (harness/variants/constrained.yaml; evidence §I), with max_open 25 while the shared cap sat at 150 for 41 of 53 hours (evidence contradiction 4). In A the key was decided on the fresher intent and in B the intent carries a cap_gate row, so neither is a silent lost decision; both are the same class journal 79 ruled on ("a check defect, not an integrity anomaly"). Residual (unverified): a Place failing inside its own savepoint (loop.py _apply) also leaves a bare intent, but it is logged and recorded in heartbeat.last_error, and journals 101/107 report no executor error on 09-10. The split of the 483 between A and B is unverified (evidence.md has no order_events counts by kind); the mechanism refutation and the storm exclusion are code- and journal-certain.

materiality: The count is real (evidence I: intents_without_order_or_skip fail 483 at 2026-09-11 09:15:53Z, after 0 fails at the 04:25 CT 09-10 sweep, journal.md:1196), but the finding mis-times it and over-weights it. (1) Timing: the 24 h window is 04:15 CT 09-10 to 04:15 CT 09-11; the last intent was created 00:51 CT 09-11 (brief) and journal 109 says explicitly "no new intents inside the window, the executor placed nothing at 03:00", so zero of the 483 can sit in the 03:15-04:15 deploy/dump storm the recommendation tells the owner to histogram; the only executor downtime in the window was 05:20-05:24 CT (journal 110, 4 min < the 900 s TTL) with no intents alive. (2) Mechanism: a better-fitting silent path than TTL age-out is same-loop supersession. insert_intents writes one intent per candidate signal at the loop's now (store.py:207-231); _NEWEST_INTENTS is `distinct on (variant_id, venue_market_id, side)` ordered by signal_created_at desc (store.py:257-268), so when a loop runs 100-256 s (evidence D2: 18:00-21:00 CT 09-10 p95 101-115 s, max 256 s) against a pricer emitting a new signal per key every 1-3.5 min (evidence F), the older sibling intents are inserted and never loaded, and no Skip is ever emitted for them (plan.py:519-556 only sees the newest); the check excuses a key only when an order was working on it (checks.py:190-217), so keys blocked by the 150 cap (evidence D3: pinned at 150 from 08:00 CT 09-10 through 00:00 CT 09-11) get an exec_capacity skip on the newest intent and a check hit on each older sibling. Both mechanisms are inferred, but this one is consistent with every timestamp in the evidence and the reviewer's is not. (3) Materiality: under either mechanism nothing economic is lost, since the newer intent on the same key carries the same market/side to the same decision chain, and 483 is ~1.6 % of a day's intents; the weekly funnel already counts "intents that reached a decision rather than the intents that were written" (harness/report/tables.py:36-37, fix 31), so the recommended funnel exclusion is already in place. The residual cost is the one journal.md:1041 named when the check was first corrected: a by-design silent path the check does not model turns the Pulse invariant wall red on every slow game night and a genuinely lost intent would hide behind that same fail. That is a check-definition defect (gate 13: a hotfix never changes a check) for phase 6's design list, not evidence that the NAS is losing intents, and it should not move the owner's viability, quality, or Mac mini decision in the next two weeks.

refuted_findings.title: The Monday replay-vs-live 2 % band will measure host latency, not integrity
refuted_findings.claim: R14's Monday duty replays the last game day on a clean 15 s grid with `now` injected and expects live order and fill counts within 2 %; the live executor ran at 27-118 s loops on Thursday and will on Sat/Sun, so the replay will place, cancel and fill on a different clock and the band is likely to fail for host reasons. That is useful (it is the one instrument that quantifies how much the host changed the experiment) but must not be read as an integrity anomaly.
reasons:
alternative: The claim's premise (replay on a 15 s grid vs live loops of 27-118 s) is real, but its attribution ("will fail for host reasons"; "the one instrument that quantifies how much the host changed the experiment") is not supported by the code. The replay path differs from live in at least four design-structural ways that would move order and fill counts on a perfect host, so a miss outside the band cannot be read as host latency:

1. Cap scope. `exec_max_open_orders` 150 is counted over every working order regardless of variant (harness/execution/plan.py:589-609 `still_open` over all `open_orders`; harness/execution/store.py:336 `_WORKING_ORDERS` filters only `o.replay`, no variant), but the replay executor is built with `variants=[variant.variant_id]` (harness/replay.py `_execute`), so a single-variant replay has the whole 150 to itself while live sharp_direct competed with sharp_two_sided and constrained. The cap bound on Thursday: 150 resting at 20:35 CT and "1,466 orders placed and cancelled ... to arrive at 150 resting" (brief; phase 5 report). Replay orders for one variant would exceed live for that reason alone, independent of the host.

2. Signal clock offset. Live signals are stamped at `pricing_now = self.clock()` taken before pricing (harness/recorder/tick.py:911, :920), while `finished_at` is stamped at the end of the tick (tick.py:962; recorder/store.py:29). `pricing_clock_for_run` returns `finished_at` (harness/strategy/pipeline.py:126-127), and replay stamps its signals with it (replay.py, `_insert_signals(..., clock, ...)`). Journal 57 records daytime ticks of 50-148 s, so every replayed signal appears 50-148 s after its live twin: the same order of magnitude as the loop latency the claim blames, and present on any host. The strict-equality test only holds because its fixture sets `finished_at` to the exact instant it prices with (tests/test_replay_execute.py:58-60, :124, :137).

3. Re-scoring, not replaying, signals. `replay()` calls `run_strategy` on `_load_gap_rows` for every run with snapshots (replay.py), whereas the live tick skips rotated secondaries when `price_budget_s` is exhausted (pipeline.py lines 64-79 of `price_and_signal`, `variants_skipped`; journal 56-57: 83 of 272 runs exhausted; journal 92: `budget_exhausted` x9 still on 2026-09-10). Amendment 4 protects the primary (sharp_direct) and gate (sharp_two_sided) but `constrained` is a secondary (harness/variants/constrained.yaml:3), so its replay scores runs live never scored.

4. Fill counting. `_REPLAY_COUNTS` (replay.py) counts every fill method, and live fills are 646/724 no_watcher counterfactual rows vs 2 queue_model (brief). The no_watcher track runs to `deadline = min(now, expiry)` (harness/execution/loop.py ~867-871), so in replay the track is truncated at the grid's last instant (`_execute` stops at `pricing_clock_for_run(to_run)`) while live keeps simulating to expiry: orders placed late in the range carry fewer replay fills by construction. A 2 % band on a count that is 89 % counterfactual rows says little about paper-fill integrity either way.

Also: no code computes the live-vs-replay 2 % comparison. `_replay_row_counts` returns replay counts only; harness/ops/checks.py has no replay-vs-live check (its replay mentions are `replay = false` filters at lines 142-271), and docs/superpowers/autopilot/verify.md has no replay-vs-live row (only `replay=false` filters at lines 54-308) despite spec line 131 promising one. The duty has never run on real data (journal 631: the one NAS replay was signals-only for Amendment 3; journal 133: duty n/a before phase 3). The adversarial review itself sized the band to "tolerate a WS gap during the day" (docs/superpowers/reviews/2026-09-07-autopilot-adversarial-review.md:201), i.e. data gaps, not host latency, and the roadmap's "integrity anomaly" wording (roadmap.md:305) is the ruling R14 (review line 272). Store.py:18-29 additionally records that match/kickoff state reads current values in replay (review M7), a stated limitation.

Net: a Monday miss outside 2 % is most plausibly explained by the cap-scope and clock-offset mismatches (present on any host) and cannot be decomposed into a host component; the claim's "useful instrument for host impact" characterization is therefore refuted, while its narrower point that a miss is not by itself an integrity anomaly survives with a different reason.

materiality: The mechanism is real but the finding is a prediction about a duty that has never run in the field, and even if it comes true it changes nothing the owner decides in the next 1-2 weeks. Evidence: (1) The R14 test proves equality only under an identical clock: tests/test_replay_execute.py:192-200 steps the "live" twin on the same fake 15 s grid; harness/replay.py:_Grid never skips a step, while the live loop stamps `now` at step start (harness/execution/loop.py:266) and counts missed grid points (loop.py:1213 `_loops_skipped`; loops_skipped 354 -> 424 on Thu, journal 101/107). So placement instants will differ on a slow host. (2) But daily ORDER counts are largely insensitive to that: an intent lives 900 s (exec_intent_ttl_s) versus a 163 s worst loop, so every intent still gets placed once and cancelled fair_stale once (7,825 of 7,997 cancels, median 12.2 min in book, brief); the count the band can plausibly miss is FILLS, where queue_model has 1 order all-time and no_watcher 646 rows, plus the 150-cap ordering effect when the cap binds (Thu 20:35, brief). Magnitude unverified either way. (3) The duty has never been evaluated: journal 133 marks it n/a; the only field replay (Amendment 3, 2026-09-08, journal 50 and reports/2026-09-08-stopped-0505.md:35) was signal-only, no `--execute`, 12,010 candidates over 198 runs. (4) The owner planned the Mac mini migration for today (brief; roadmap.md User-side TODO, journal 102); if Sunday runs on the new host the premise (27-118 s loops on Sat/Sun) does not apply to Monday's duty at all. (5) Consequence if the band does miss on the NAS: roadmap.md:305 makes it "an integrity anomaly, not a headline", i.e. one autopilot investigation unit and a line in the week-1 report; it touches no paper P&L, no gate row (gate reads live tables, spec §4), and does not move the Mac mini decision, whose trigger is already met (journal 101). The constructive half (replay Thu 2026-09-10, runs of that day, as a NAS-latency estimate before/after the host move) is a useful note for the loop but is info-level, not "important".

title: Host decision: NAS as-is, NAS upgraded, or Mac mini
summary: Not clear. The evidence supports "stay and tune, then measure", not "move now". The two catastrophic regimes are gone: the 16-container media stack (journal 101/102: 5 GB swap, memory-pressure full 16 %, loop avg 27.5 s / p95 118 s in the 19:00 hour) and unsummarized BRINs (journal 93: 39.6 s to 2.8 ms). What remains after the media stop is IO wait 16-20 % with swap-out 0 (journal 107) and p95 9.1-15.2 s late Thursday against the 7.5 s row (verify.md:117): cold reads on a single-member rotational RAID1 (evidence A) holding a 47 GB database behind ~3.9 GB of page cache and shared_buffers 512 MB; Postgres read 1.89 TB from disk in 3 days. On 09-09 (no game, media running, warm cache) the same box passed at p95 6.19 s (D1). The roadmap's own trigger (roadmap:315) needs two consecutive game windows over 7.5 s with fixes 31-32; Thursday was the first, Friday 18:00 CT is the second. Cheapest fix: WD SN850X 2 TB ($156) in a free M.2 PCIe 4 slot as a UGOS pool for pgdata (~30-45 min stop), then 2x16 GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM ($280-450) to 32 GB. Two hard facts change the calculus regardless of host: (1) /volume1 is at 69 % used and dump.sh skips nightly backups below 30 % free (Use% >= 71), which the 8 GB/day growth reaches about 2026-09-27 (range 09-21 to 10-03), after which Makefile:65 aborts every full deploy; (2) the executor's warm cost at 150 resting orders is already p50 7.6-7.9 s (D2 16:00/17:00/22:00), so no host alone passes the 7.5 s row until the loop's per-order tape reads are bounded. Mac mini: RAM unknown; needs >= 16 GB, native Postgres on an external SSD, auto-login (FileVault off), and a full logical dump/restore (the nightly dump has no tape). Cutover, if any: Tue 2026-09-15 08:00-16:00 CT.

Measure the second window tonight (Fri 18:00 CT) and the Saturday slate with the media containers stopped and the deployed research switches as they are (7c3d555): hourly exec.loop_ms p50/p95 and exec.open_orders, vmstat 5 3 (si/so/wa), /proc/pressure/io, and pg_stat_database blks_hit vs blks_read at 17:00, 19:00, 21:00, 23:00 CT. Decision rule: p95 <= 7.5 s in every hour with open_orders >= 100 -> stay, buy nothing for latency; p95 > 7.5 s with si/so ~0 and wa >= 15 % -> disk-bound -> NVMe pgdata (H3); si/so > 0 with media stopped -> RAM (H4); p95 > 7.5 s with wa < 5 % and si/so 0 -> the loop's own cost (H5), no host change helps.
corrections: After the media stop the executor's residual is IO wait on cold page-cache misses against a rotational disk (journal 107: IO wait 16-20 %, swap-out 0, evening half-hour p95 9.1-15.2 s), no longer swap thrash; but those misses are a function of RAM as well as disk (47 GB database, 3.9 GB buff/cache, 7.7 GB RAM, 1.87 GB still swapped, swap-in 139-781 pages/5 s at 23:17). The two regimes behind the Thursday collapse are addressed, not closed: the media containers are stopped (docker stop, restart policy unless-stopped, journal 102) and BRIN autosummarize is live (journal 93/98); deploy cold-cache storms (91-129 s) and the 03:30 pg_dump + RFQ replay (235-336 s, journal 109; D1 09-11 max 335,763) remain. The NAS has never passed the 7.5 s p95 row in a game window: 09-09 SEA-NE window p95 7,956 ms (journal 96, pre-fixes 31-32); the 6,188 ms figure is the 09-09 whole-day p95. It has passed in quiet daytime (journal 96: p95 4,474 ms, IO wait 0-1 %). The roadmap trigger (roadmap.md:315) has three OR'd clauses; journal 101 met the swap clause, which the media stop removed (journal 107, evidence A si 2 so 0); the two-consecutive-windows clause with fixes 31-32 (deployed 09-10 06:36/07:13 CT) has one measured window (Thu), which stayed over 7.5 s even after the media stop (D2: 22:00 p95 13.2 s, 23:00 p95 9.0 s); Fri 18:00 CT is the second. The move is not proven by the roadmap's own literal test, but the Thursday post-stop numbers and the RAM-limited cache make it likely to be met tonight.

The move is not yet proven by the roadmap's two-window clause (one window, Thu LAR-SF, measured with fixes 31-32; Fri 2026-09-11 18:00 CT is the second), but the trigger is disjunctive and fired on the swap clause at 20:10 CT (roadmap.md:315, journal 101: swap-out 1.49 MB/s, 5 GB resident, IO wait 25-32 %), and the roadmap's standard is "flag, user decides", not proof. No game window has passed the 7.5 s p95 row: Wed 09-09 SEA-NE in-window p95 7,956 ms (journal 92 addendum, journal.md:1227; the daily 6,188 ms in evidence.md D1 is a whole-day aggregate, not an in-window pass) and Thu 09-10 LAR-SF 118 s in the 19:00 hour, 9.1-15.2 s per half hour after the media stop (journal 107, evidence.md D2). The post-media-stop residual is IO wait on a growing database read from a single rotational HDD (journal 107; evidence.md A: pgdata on sda ROTA=1, 1.89 TB read in 3 days; DB 47 GB growing 8.94 GB/day against 3.9 GB page cache), and the NAS has no in-place disk remedy (NVMe 119 GB, 109 GB overlay; archive/drop is user gate U3), so "disk, not RAM" changes what the alternate host must supply (NVMe plus RAM), not whether a move is warranted. The swap regime is avoided, not fixed: it returns if the 16 media containers are started again (journal 102; R17 assumed co-tenancy). Part of the residual is executor design (150 resting orders x tape reads per 15 s loop; journal 107 "the loop needs its own budget"), which a faster host masks rather than fixes and belongs in phase 6 regardless of host. Severity: major (decision quality), not critical; the Friday window gives a clean second reading before the user must act, and the Mac mini's own storage/RAM are unverified in the repo.

Severity MAJOR (not critical), question host: the roadmap trigger is no longer met on the swap clause after the media stop and has only one of its two game windows, so the Mac mini move planned for 2026-09-11 should be deferred past the weekend slate and decided on the Fri 18:00 CT and Saturday measurements (hourly exec.loop_ms p50/p95 with open_orders >= 100, vmstat si/so/wa, /proc/pressure/io, blks_hit vs blks_read); major rather than critical because a Mac mini fixes both the disk and RAM hypotheses so mis-diagnosis is cheap, the 'NVMe pgdata on the NAS' branch is infeasible (119 GB NVMe vs a 47 GB DB growing ~9 GB/day), the 09-09 pass was a no-game day, and the host is second-order to the experiment's real bottleneck (fair_stale churn and the 150-order cap).

corrections: The DXP4800 Pro (i3-1315U per evidence A lscpu) ships 8 GB DDR5-5600 in one of two SODIMM slots, vendor-rated expandable to 96 GB (the DXP4800 Plus, a different model with DDR5-4800, is rated 64 GB per TechPowerUp); a single Crucial CT16G56C46S5 16 GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM is $144.99 at crucial.com (-> 24 GB; the $219.99 Best Buy figure is unverified), and 32 GB (2x16 GB) DDR5 kits start at $350-399 per Tom's Hardware's price index (desktop kits; the $280-449 SODIMM endpoints are unverified). With 32 GB the harness could run shared_buffers 6-8 GB / effective_cache_size ~20 GB; at today's sizes (evidence C) that holds roughly the last 2 days of tape (~7.5 GB/day, from 9.5 GB at journal 92 to 17 GB now) plus signals (8.8 GB, growing ~2.7 GB/day) and fair_values (1.5 GB), not 3 days, and the fit erodes at ~9 GB/day database growth (db.growth_gb_per_day 8.94), so 64 GB is the durable option; the media containers (~1.3 GiB, journal 101) could return. The harness's own containers use ~1.8 GiB (postgres 1.24 GiB + five apps 0.57 GiB, evidence A). The buff/cache 3,864 MB (of which 550 MB is shared memory) against a 47 GB database is a necessary cause of Postgres reading 1.89 TB from disk over its 3-day uptime (~630 GB/day, ~13x the database), alongside the specific read patterns the journal names (unindexed dashboard scans, fix 25; nightly dump churn, journal 964; cold-cache deploy storms, journal 109-110). Stopping the media stack freed ~1.5 GB (used 6,660 -> 5,137 MB) and cut swap 5,021 -> 2,485 MB: journal 102, not 101.

The DXP4800 Pro ships 8 GB DDR5-5600 in two SODIMM slots (64 GB on the Plus; two reviews state 96 GB for the Pro; Intel spec-sheet ceiling and current SODIMM prices unverified from the repo). Upgrading to 24-32 GB (shared_buffers 6-8 GB, effective_cache_size ~20 GB; docker-compose.yml:16-18 and shm_size at :33 change, a full deploy under R4 with a cold-restart storm) would absorb, but not remove, the read amplification that produced Postgres's 1.89 TB of block reads in 3 days. That volume comes mostly from (a) the executor's design of rescanning prints with no cursor from min(placed_at)-60 s on every 15 s loop (loop.py:677-679, R9) while cancelled orders stay 'working' until kickoff-10 min through the no_watcher track (store.py:341-349, loop.py:1173-1182), so each ticker's window widens for days (journal 102 addendum: 4,517 rows / 2,650 buffers per loop on one ticker); (b) discrete query-shape storms already fixed (22, 26, 31, 32, 35, 36, 38) and three nightly pg_dumps. A print watermark and retention would cut the reads on any RAM size. Today's hot set (~18-21 GB) fits a 20 GB cache only for about a week at 8.94 GB/day growth unless the U3 archive-and-drop gate is exercised. RAM does not change pgdata on the single rotational HDD (653 GB written / 3 days), random_page_cost 1.1 or effective_io_concurrency 1. Whether the media stack can return is unverified (journal 101 cites IO wait 25-32 % beside the swap). The harness's own containers use ~1.8 GiB (postgres 1.24 GiB + five apps ~0.58 GiB), which is correct.

Severity important (host, Q4): adding one 16 GB DDR5-5600 SO-DIMM (24 GB total; the DXP4800 family has two slots, 64 GB official; whether the Pro's 8 GB is one module is unverified, check UGOS Hardware before ordering) is the cheapest and least disruptive host lever and should be weighed against the Mac mini migration before the week-2 game window; it is the FIRST NAS-side lever, not second after the NVMe, because the 119 GB NVMe cannot hold a 47 GB database growing 8.94 GB/day; the 1.89 TB read figure is contaminated by since-fixed defects (BRIN fix 32, builder fix 31, dashboard fix 25, RFQ fix 35) and three full pg_dumps, so measure the post-fix read rate and swap-in on tonight's game before treating cache size as the proven cause; retune shared_buffers/effective_cache_size after the install; keep the media containers stopped for the rest of the experiment regardless, since their damage was IO, not RAM.

verified_findings.title: Mac mini requirements and unknowns: RAM size is the gating fact; macOS needs auto-login, native Postgres on an external SSD, and fsync_writethrough
verified_findings.claim: A Mac mini works as the host only if it has >= 16 GB (native Homebrew Postgres 16 with shared_buffers ~4 GB plus a 2-3 GB Docker VM for the five app containers, ~0.6 GiB RSS) and better at 24-32 GB; an 8 GB M1/M2 mini is no better than the tuned NAS on memory. Its internal 256 GB base SSD cannot hold the tape (150-200 GB by 09-28, ~1 TB by January), so a 2 TB external USB4/TB4 NVMe (~$156 drive + enclosure, or a finished OWC/Samsung unit; enclosure prices unverified) is required. Docker Desktop and OrbStack are user-session apps that start at login, not boot, so the mini needs auto-login, which macOS disables while FileVault is on; brew services registers a LaunchAgent (login) not a LaunchDaemon. Docker Desktop's VM defaults to 50 % of host RAM and its bind mounts run at 25-40 % of native (OrbStack 75-95 %), so pgdata must be a named volume or native, never the bind mount docker-compose.yml uses today. PostgreSQL recommends wal_sync_method=fsync_writethrough on macOS to defeat write caching, at a write-throughput cost. Power: 4-7 W idle, 39-140 W max, 10-35 C operating.

verified_findings.recommendation: Before any move, the owner states the mini's chip, RAM and SSD. Require: >= 16 GB; Postgres 16 native (brew) with data on the external SSD and wal_sync_method=fsync_writethrough; OrbStack or Docker Desktop with the VM capped at 3 GB and the disk image on the external SSD; auto-login on with FileVault off (or accept manual login after every power event); pmset autorestart 1, sleep 0. If the mini has 8 GB, stop here: tune the NAS instead.
corrections: A Mac mini works as the host only if it has >= 16 GB (native Homebrew Postgres 16 with shared_buffers ~4 GB plus a 2-3 GB Docker VM for the six app-* containers, ~0.6 GiB RSS today) and better at 24-32 GB; an 8 GB M1/M2 mini matches the 7.7 GB NAS on memory, though its NVMe would still beat the NAS's rotational pgdata on IO. The M4's 256 GB base SSD cannot hold the tape: 47 GB today growing 6-9 GB/day (evidence.md D5: 8.94) gives ~150-200 GB by 09-28 and 0.7-1.05 TB by January if the roadmap's phase 6 archive-and-drop proposal (>500 GB or <40 % free) is declined, so a 2 TB external USB4/TB4 NVMe is required (drive ~$156 and OWC Express 1M2 enclosure prices unverified). Docker Desktop and OrbStack start at user login, not boot (docker/for-mac #4388, closed; orbstack #1767: cannot run as root), so as long as the app containers run under either, the mini needs auto-login, which macOS disables while FileVault is on. Native Postgres itself does not need that: `sudo brew services start` registers a LaunchDaemon (boot); only non-sudo registers a LaunchAgent (login). Docker Desktop's VM defaults to 50 % of host RAM, and macOS bind mounts are slow (OrbStack claims 75-95 % of native for its own; a Docker Desktop percentage is unverified), so pgdata must be native or a named volume, never the bind mount docker-compose.yml:9 uses today. PostgreSQL recommends wal_sync_method=fsync_writethrough on macOS to defeat write caching, at a write-throughput cost. Power: 4-7 W idle, 39-140 W max (Apple 103253); 10-35 C operating (Apple 121555).

The Mac mini's RAM and SSD size are unknown in the repo and must be checked first (the M4/256 GB figures are assumptions). The mini's decisive advantage over the tuned NAS is storage latency, not RAM: after the media stop the NAS is no longer memory-bound (journal 107: pressure 0.89 %, brief: ~0) and every remaining storm is IO wait (journal 109-110: 34-43 %), which an internal or TB4/USB4 NVMe removes at any RAM size; the roadmap trigger (roadmap.md:315) is no longer met on swap and the p95 ceiling is red for one window, not two, so the move is the user's preference rather than a forced one, provided the media stack stays stopped. The harness effectively has ~5 GB on the NAS (7.7 GB minus ~2.8-3.7 GB UGOS, journal 101 / brief), so an 8 GB mini is roughly equal if Docker Desktop hosts the apps and somewhat better if they run natively (the CLI already anticipates macOS: settings.py:96-99, housekeeping.py:224-233); 16 GB or more is comfortable, 24-32 GB is page cache for a DB that will exceed any RAM regardless. Storage: the 3-week experiment needs ~170 GB by 09-28; a season without archive needs ~1 TB (F19); a 1 TB external with the roadmap's 500 GB archive-and-drop trigger (phase 6 item 7) suffices, 2 TB matches ruling U3's ceiling; a single external SSD gives the tape no redundancy (F66), unlike the NAS RAID. Boot: native Postgres via `sudo brew services` starts at boot as a system-wide service (Homebrew manpage); only Docker-hosted app containers need a login session, and auto-login conflicts with FileVault only if FileVault is enabled. pgdata should be native or a named volume, not the compose bind mount, and app-run's /pgdata-ro statvfs mount (compose:81), verify.md's /volume1 and free -m rows (verify.md:66,82-83), app-backup's service-name host (compose:49) and the deploy recipe (Makefile:15-75) all need host-specific changes. wal_sync_method=fsync_writethrough is an option to defeat write caching, not a recommendation; the NAS runs without it today (compose:13-32), and its cost on 4M-rows/hour ingest and its behaviour through a USB enclosure bridge are unverified. Moving the tape needs a pgdata copy or bulk-inclusive dump, since the nightly dump excludes the five bulk tables (F66).

Severity important (question: host). Before migrating, the owner states the mini's chip, RAM and SSD; the repo holds no record of them (unverified). Gate: if the mini has 8 GB, do not move: the NAS after the media stop is at memory pressure ~0 with 2,983 MB available and swap resident 1,858 MB (brief; journal 107), and an 8 GB mini running Docker Desktop's default 50 %-of-RAM VM (Docker docs; memory file laptop-memory-constraints, 4.1 GB measured) is no better. If >= 16 GB, the move only helps under three conditions: (a) Postgres data on a named volume or native brew Postgres, never the './pgdata' host bind mount at docker-compose.yml:9 (Docker Desktop bind mounts 25-40 % of native per OrbStack's benchmark); (b) a 2 TB external NVMe, because 47 GB growing 6-8 GB/day reaches 149-183 GB by 09-28 and U3's 2 TB ceiling (roadmap.md:39) far exceeds a 256 GB base SSD; (c) auto-login with FileVault off plus pmset autorestart, since Docker Desktop/OrbStack and brew services start at login, not boot. Demote to info: power/thermal figures, enclosure prices, and wal_sync_method=fsync_writethrough (a durability nicety for a paper-mode experiment with a nightly pg_dump).

verified_findings.title: The migration cannot use the backup/restore drill: the nightly dump excludes the tape, so a full logical dump/restore (1-2 h, unverified) or a shut-down file copy is required, plus a Kalshi tape gap with no replay
verified_findings.claim: The nightly dump excludes raw_responses, orderbook_events, venue_trades, venue_quotes and odds_snapshots (~36 GB of the 47), so the memory file's plan 'Postgres data copy via the backup/restore drill' would drop the tape, the fills' print evidence and the R14 replay-vs-live duty; the supported path to a different architecture and libc (x86_64 glibc container -> arm64 macOS) is a full pg_dump/pg_restore (indexes rebuilt under the target collation), which is hours not minutes; a file-level copy needs the server shut down and, into a native macOS Postgres, changes the collation provider under every text btree (ticker keys) so a REINDEX would follow; the Kalshi socket re-sends an orderbook_snapshot only on (re)subscribe, so deltas during the gap are lost (counted as gap rows); on resume every resting order's fair is older than the 220 s allowance, so the first priced loop mass-cancels on fair_stale.

verified_findings.recommendation: If the move happens: rehearse the timing first by restoring last night's nightly plus a one-off full dump into the mini in the quiet hour; choose logical dump/restore (pg_dump -Fd -j 4 on the NAS, pg_restore -j 8 on the mini) and accept a tape gap of the restore's length unless app-ws is left recording on the NAS and the tape partitions are copied after (two-step copy). Correct the memory file. Expect a fair_stale mass cancel on the first tick and log it as expected, not as a defect.
corrections: The nightly dump excludes raw_responses, orderbook_events, venue_trades, venue_quotes and odds_snapshots (35.9 GB of the 47 GB: evidence.md C; backups.md:3-6; dump.sh:57-61), and the restore drill restores exactly one nightly .dump (drill.sh:21,129-133), so the memory file's plan 'Postgres data copy via the backup/restore drill' would leave behind the live orderbook_events partition (17 GB, unsealed until Monday 04:00 CT), the 15 GB legacy partition and the other three bulk tables (3.2 GB), and with them the fills' print evidence and the Monday replay-vs-live duty (R14, roadmap:305). Only sealed weekly orderbook_events/venue_trades partitions have any archive (backups/partitions/, backups.md:109-112), and nothing restores them into the drill. Moving to a different architecture (x86_64 container -> arm64) means a full pg_dump/pg_restore of the tape (hours, unverified) or a shut-down file-level copy (PG 16 file-system backup requires the server stopped; cross-architecture copy unsupported, unverified); the collation-provider/REINDEX concern applies only if the target is a native macOS Postgres, not the planned 'Docker on macOS' postgres:16 image. The Kalshi socket re-sends an orderbook_snapshot only on (re)subscribe (ws.py:210-212; ws_sink.py:49), so tape during the stop is lost and counted as gap rows (journal 109: ~3.5 min of tape for one app-ws recreate). On resume, cold loops run 90-130 s (journal 109/110) and any resting order's fair is older than the fixed 220 s allowance (fair.py:24,30; settings.py:26; evidence G), so the first loop cancels them on fair_stale (plan.py:446,501); this is code-verified, not yet observed at a restart, and low-cost for paper orders (7,825 of 7,997 already end fair_stale).

The memory file's plan 'Postgres data copy via the backup/restore drill' cannot carry the tape: the nightly and weekly dumps exclude raw_responses, orderbook_events, venue_trades, venue_quotes and odds_snapshots (deploy/backup/dump.sh:57-61; ~36 GB of the 47 GB, evidence C), and no partition archive exists yet (loop.sh:13,43-48 archives only the previous sealed ISO week on Monday 04:00 CT; partitioning began Mon 09-08, so legacy 15 GB and w37 17 GB are RAID-only; raw_responses, venue_quotes and odds_snapshots are never archived). Restoring the nightly dump alone already takes ~2 h on the NAS (journal lines 983, 1081: 'two hours, most of it index builds'), so a full logical dump/restore of 47 GB is hours (exact figure unverified). Because the recorded plan is 'Docker on macOS' (memory file line 12) with the same postgres:16 image (docker-compose.yml:3), a shut-down file-level copy of pgdata into the arm64 container keeps the glibc collation provider and needs no REINDEX on that ground; the shutdown itself is required and the deploy recipe never stops postgres (Makefile:65,73,75), while x86_64 -> aarch64 data-directory compatibility is unverified. The Kalshi tape gap during the move is the same bounded, journaled gap every deploy already produces (journal 109: 3.5 min; journal 110: two more recreates), handled by gap rows, dirty books, re-anchoring and queue truncation (ws_sink.py:93-99, book.py:93-114, loop.py:829-836) under ruling R14; it drops the Monday replay-vs-live duty only if the move spans a game day. On resume, resting orders older than the 220 s allowance are cancelled fair_stale by design (F36; plan.py:446-456), the same drain seen nightly (evidence D4: 150 cancelled/0 placed at 01:00 CT 09-10); the no_watcher track continues to expiry (loop.py:21-23), so the cost is the watched track on 0 orders (overnight/early-morning move; open_orders 0 now) to at most 150 (daytime move, D3), and whether the recorder's first tick re-prices before the executor's first cold loop is unverified. Migration therefore needs a shut-down file copy or a full pg_dump/pg_restore scheduled outside a game window, not the nightly drill.

Severity: important (question: host). The memory file's migration method (nightly backup/restore drill) would discard ~36 GB of the 47 GB database, including the whole orderbook/trade tape that the experiment's dataset, the fills' print evidence and the Monday R14 replay duty depend on, and the only supported cross-architecture path is a full logical pg_dump/pg_restore whose duration on this NAS is unmeasured but likely multiple hours (the non-bulk 1 GB drill restore alone took ~113 min), so the owner should not migrate today before kickoff: rehearse the full dump timing first, run the move in a quiet window (or after the Monday 04:00 CT w37 partition archive), and correct the memory file; the Kalshi tape gap and the first-tick fair_stale cancels are expected, minor costs of any quiet-hour move (precedent journal 43; 0 orders rest overnight).

verified_findings.title: Decision table: stay-and-tune beats both hybrids and matches the full move on expected p95 at a fraction of the risk
verified_findings.claim: Options with cost, downtime, risk and expected game-night p95 (estimates, labelled): (1) status quo, media stopped: $0, 0 downtime, low risk, p95 9-15 s measured late Thu and est 10-25 s in the busiest hour, FAILS the row; (2) NVMe pgdata on the NAS: $156, one 30-45 min stack stop, low risk (single SSD, no redundancy, same as today's single-member RAID1), est p95 4-8 s, also removes H2; (3) RAM to 24/32 GB: $145-450, ~15 min power cycle, low risk, est 5-9 s, media may return; (4) both plus a Postgres retune: $300-600, one ~60 min window, low risk, est 3-6 s; (5) Mac mini full move: $0 if the mini has >= 16 GB plus $250-400 external SSD, a day of setup and a 15 min-2 h tape gap, medium-high risk (RAM unknown, login-session daemons, mount semantics, collation, cross-arch, rollback), est 3-5 s with native Postgres, worse than (4) if the mini has 8 GB; (6) hybrid B (Postgres on the mini, apps on the NAS): same SSD cost and gap, medium risk (Postgres on the LAN with the harness:harness password, statvfs on the wrong disk, per-query LAN RTT), est 4-8 s; (7) hybrid A (apps on the mini, Postgres on the NAS HDD): no change, the IO wait is inside Postgres, not recommended.

Decision table, estimates labelled: (1) status quo, media stopped: $0, 0 downtime, p95 measured 9.1-15.2 s in the late Thu half hours (journal 107) and 11.5-15.2 s while LAR-SF was still in play after the stop, est 10-25 s in the busiest hour; fails the 7.5 s ceiling (roadmap User-side TODO). (4) both plus a Postgres retune (random_page_cost 1.1, effective_io_concurrency 1, wal_compression off, effective_cache_size 1.5 GB per evidence.md B): est 3-6 s, one window; recommended over the hybrids on the evidence. (5) Mac mini full move: RAM unknown (memory file records no specs), cross-arch and collation force a dump/restore path that excludes the five bulk tables (backups.md:72), a day of setup, medium-high risk; est 3-5 s, possibly lower than (4) because the loop's quiet-day floor (p95 4.5-6.2 s, D1 09-09, journal 96) is Python and per-ticker query RTT rather than disk. (6) hybrid B: medium risk, est 4-8 s. (7) hybrid A: no change, the IO wait is inside Postgres. Caveat for every option: the executor's idle loop grew from p95 4.8 s (09-10 07:00, journal 101) to p50 5.3 s / avg 9.7 s with zero open orders (D1 09-11) because working_orders keeps every cancelled order with nw_done = false until expiry (store.py:336, loop.py:866) and rescans prints from placed_at - 60 s each loop (loop.py:678), so p95 on any host tracks fair_stale churn and tape growth (8.94 GB/day); the host decision should be paired with the phase 4.5 report's unanswered cadence/staleness question and the phase 6 archive-and-drop item.

Severity important (not critical): it reverses a migration the owner planned for today on well-evidenced mechanism (IO on rotational pgdata is the residual after the media stop), but the option 2-7 p95 figures and the NAS slot availability are unmeasured, and the recommendation should state explicitly that no hardware option can land before the Fri/Sun games or the Mon 09-14 gate, so the near-term choice is status quo vs a risky same-day move, with NVMe -> RAM as the week-2 path.

refuted_findings.title: At 150 resting orders the loop's warm cost is already p50 7.6-7.9 s; no host alone passes the 7.5 s row until the executor's per-order reads are bounded
refuted_findings.claim: The 150-order cap (exec_max_open_orders, shared) was binding in 41 of 53 hours with open orders; in those hours the median loop was 7.6-7.9 s even without the swap storm (16:00, 17:00 and 22:00 CT on 09-10), because each resting order costs a tape read by ticker plus watcher writes (order_watch_samples 228,510 rows), so the loop's own work scales with resting orders and the 7.5 s p95 ceiling (half the 15 s period) is marginal on any host; journal 107 already says 'the loop needs its own budget'.
reasons: evidence: Three load-bearing parts fail. (1) Count: evidence.md D3 lists 53 hours and only 36 have max = 150 (counted from the table); "41 of 53" comes from controller note 4, which misstates its own D3 data. (2) Mechanism: harness/execution/loop.py:697-724 keys the tape read on row.ticker (one load_prints + load_deltas per ticker, not per order), and the working set (harness/execution/store.py:336, `status in open/partially_filled or nw_done = false`) includes cancelled orders whose no_watcher counterfactual track is still running, so the read count tracks distinct tickers across open plus counterfactual tracks, not the 150 cap; watcher writes are one row per open order per watch_sample_s = 60 s (settings.py:94; loop.py:1088-1103), ~150 rows/min at the cap, not a per-loop cost. The journal 102 addendum's 6.3 ms warm read is real but the "x 150 orders" multiplication is the reviewer's own and does not follow from the code. (3) Attribution: the same evidence shows ~150 resting orders at p50 ~5 s during 09-10 daytime (D3 10:00-13:00 max 150, hourly averages 128.5/78.6/90.5/144.0; journal 101: those hours avg 5.1-5.8 s p95 7.8-9.8 s; D1 09-10 p50 5,189 ms). The 16:00/17:00 p50 of 7.8-7.9 s coincides with 4-6x the placement churn (D4: 335 and 441 placed, 335 and 591 cancelled, versus 78 at 13:00) and with rising memory pressure (journal 101: 16:00 avg 9.5 s p95 23.5 s; D2 16:00 p95 21.3 s max 26.6 s is not a clean hour), and 22:00 (p50 7.6 s) was the post-swap recovery at IO wait 16-20 % (journal 107). "Without the swap storm" for 16:00-17:00 is unverified: no per-hour memory readings exist before 20:07 CT. Verified as correct: D2 p50s, D1 p50s, D3 150.0 averages in 21:00/22:00 on 09-08 and 09-10, journal 107 verdict text, verify.md:117 ceiling = exec_period_s (settings.py:54, 15 s) x 1000 / 2, loop.py:1237 EXEC_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000, order_watch_samples 228,510 rows (evidence C). Controller note 3 independently supports the weaker point that only 09-09 passed the 7.5 s p95 row.

alternative: Three premises fail. (1) Mechanism: harness/execution/loop.py:674-678 `_tape` does one print scan and one delta scan PER TICKER "shared by every order on it" (windows keyed by row.ticker, fix 22); the 6.3 ms figure in journal 102 addendum is a per-ticker read, and even 150 x 6.3 ms = 0.95 s, not 7.6 s. Watcher writes are one row per order per watch_sample_s=60 s (settings.py:94) in one batched insert per loop (loop.py:1088-1119); 228,510 rows / 28 MB over 3 days is ~1 row/s. (2) "Without the swap storm" is false for 16:00/17:00 on 09-10: media containers were stopped at 20:12 CT (journal 102); journal 101 at 20:07 recorded swap 5,021 MB used, swap-in/out 382/1,822 per 5 s, IO wait 25-32 %, memory pressure full avg300 16 %, and placed the 16:00 hour (avg 9.5 s, p95 23.5 s) inside the same ramp, ruling "The executor's own work is flat: dirty_markets 107-117, intents_considered 500-1,260, open_orders 53-144. Same work, five to six times the wall clock." The 22:00 hour is the non-monotonic swap-back (journal 102 addendum; journal 107: swap resident 2,253 MB, IO wait 16-20 %, 21:00 hump = hourly settlement job; half-hours 8.1 -> 7.7 -> 7.1 s falling as the cache warmed). (3) Same order count, same host, half the cost the day before: evidence D1 09-09 p50 3,013 ms / p95 6,188 ms (passes the 7.5 s row) while D3 shows the 150 cap binding in ten of 09-09's hours; journal 92 addendum SEA-NE window 09-09 19:20-23:20 (D3 open orders avg 115-138): 210 loops avg 4,885 ms p95 7,956 ms; journal 92: 09-10 00:00 CT hour avg 5.5 s at open_orders avg 95.9/max 150, on a box with BRIN not yet fixed (journal 93) and 4.5-5 GB in swap (journal 90). What survives: the 7.5 s p95 row is marginal on this NAS, but the driver is order-independent: 09-11 daytime at exec.open_orders avg 0.3 and intents_considered 0 (evidence D exec metrics 6 h) p50 5,344 ms and exec_heartbeat p95_loop_ms 7,112 at open_orders 0, versus 3.9 s avg / 4.8 s p95 at zero orders in the 09-10 07:00 hour (journal 101; D3 has no 02:00-07:00 rows). The zero-order floor grew ~1.4 s/day as the DB went 34 -> 40 -> 47 GB (8.94 GB/day, evidence C) on a rotational HDD with random_page_cost 1.1 (evidence A/B, controller note 6). The measured order-count effect on 09-10 daytime was 5.1-5.8 s at 79-144 avg open orders vs 3.9 s at zero (journal 101 + D3): ~1.2-1.9 s, ~10-15 ms per resting order, a quarter of the loop. Per-order reads are already per-ticker and batch-bounded (fixes 22/26, DELTA_BATCH_LIMIT 20,000 / floor 250, store.py:484-493), so "bound the per-order reads" is not the lever. Journal 107's full sentence names the host: "the loop needs its own budget, and the NAS's IO wait is the next limit after memory." Unverified: the exact split of the 5.3 s zero-order floor among candidate_signals (signals 14.6 M rows / 8.8 GB), newest_event_ts, market_rows and the 06:40 CT restart's cold cache; and the distinct-ticker count behind 150 resting orders at any instant (only the all-time 445 distinct (variant, market, side) is in evidence G).

materiality: The finding's mechanism and host-independence claim do not hold. (1) Tape reads are per ticker, not per order: harness/execution/loop.py:676 "One print scan and one delta scan per ticker, shared by every order on it"; watcher writes are one batched insert per loop (loop.py:1088-1119) into a 28 MB table (evidence C), so the loop does not scale linearly with 150 resting orders. (2) The same NAS passed the 7.5 s ceiling at 100-150 resting orders: evidence D1 09-09 p50 3,013 ms / p95 6,188 ms while D3 shows 09-09 hourly open_orders averages of 94-138 (08:00, 09:00, 13:00-15:00, 18:00-21:00); journal 1039 "loop p95 2.9 s ... 123 open orders"; journal 1111 "p95 4.5 s, 150 open orders"; journal 96 (line 1224) 3,839 ms avg on the 09-10 morning with 116.7 avg orders (D3). (3) The cited 7.6-7.9 s p50 hours were not "warm without the swap storm": 16:00-17:00 on 09-10 ran with the media containers still up (stopped 20:12 CT, journal 102) and 22:00 was inside the swap-back with IO wait 16-20 % and 2.25 GB resident swap (journal 107). (4) Today's idle loop with 0.3 open orders carries heartbeat p95 7,112 ms and daily p50 5,344 ms (evidence D exec_heartbeat, D1), so the zero-order floor is already ~70 % of the 7.6 s; host/DB state (47 GB DB on rotational pgdata, dirty_markets ~123) is the dominant term. What survives is journal 107's carried observation and journal 92 addendum (SEA-NE p95 7,956 ms at 114 dirty markets): a phase 6 executor-budget line and a re-measure on the new host are reasonable, but as a minor plan-next item. Rating this "important" on the host question would wrongly weaken the case for the Mac mini move, which the evidence (09-09 passing at 150 orders on the same code) does not support. Unverified: the exact per-loop cost split between tape scan, watcher insert and the pricing/dirty-market work (no profiling data in the journal).

minor_findings.title: Postgres is tuned for an SSD it does not have, no container has a memory limit, and the tape's 'RAID' is one disk
minor_findings.claim: random_page_cost 1.1 and effective_io_concurrency 1 are set for the rotational pool (the former favours index scans that seek on the HDD; both become correct after H3), effective_cache_size 1.5 GB understates the 3.9 GB cache today and would understate 32 GB badly, wal_compression is off on a write-heavy tape (653 GB written in 3 days), no sports-harness or media container has a memory or CPU limit so a returning media stack can push Postgres into swap again, and md1 is a RAID1 with a single member so the tape has no redundancy on the NAS and would have none on an external SSD either.

title: Autopilot process quality and defect escapes
summary: Defect escape: of carried fixes 21-41 (21 items), 20 were found in production (4 at a deploy step, 16 by post-deploy verify) and 1 (fix 33) by a later phase's task review after its code was already live: a 95-100 % escape rate. Cause classes: external API shape/behaviour assumed not recorded 8 (38 %), NAS performance / DB size 7 (33 %), scope surprise 2, deploy plumbing 2 (the DDL lock race recurred three times: fixes 13, 21, 37), logic 2. A recorded-fixture-through-the-production-path policy would have pre-empted 6, a $0 read-only probe at plan-next 4-5, a timing run on the drill's restored NAS-sized copy 7. Review effectiveness: opus final reviews caught 1/4/2 Criticals in phases 4/4.5/5 and hotfix reviews 4 more, all cross-task seams and code-internal correctness; none of the 20 production escapes was in that class, so SDD catches what it can see and is structurally blind to the environment. Hygiene: state.md's header has read "Updated: 2026-09-10 14:10 CT" through 20 rewrites over 17 hours; the Agents, NAS-build, Carried-fixes and Day-counter lines contradict its own Position line; 6 of 112 journal headings are stamped before their predecessor; no preflight or R3 test notification has been journaled since 2026-09-09 08:29 despite 7 deploys since. Docs: README overstates cadence ("every two minutes" vs a 15-minute pricing cadence, 243 priced ticks/day), lists two gate rules gate.py does not code and omits two it does, and says "nothing here can send an order to Kalshi" while the NAS key is write-scoped. Gates: no R4 deploy breach found in 22 deploy entries, but invariant 5 was crossed twice: fix 38's rfqs retention prune shipped on a controller amendment (0bd4b4c) with no user yes, and journal 112 deleted 4 job_state rows by hand with no ruling. Velocity: 626 commits (330 code, 296 docs) in 5.3 days, 25 production builds (~6/day), tests 265 to 2,926. Grade C+: excellent construction discipline (115 cost-if-wrong rulings), weak operating discipline.

verified_findings.title: 95-100 % of carried fixes 21-41 escaped to production; the environment classes dominate
verified_findings.claim: Of the 21 carried fixes 21-41, 20 were first found on the NAS (fixes 21, 30, 31, 37 at a deploy step; 22-29, 32, 34-36, 38-41 by post-deploy verify) and fix 33 was found by a phase 5 task review after its code (ticket.py, report_wtd.py) was already live from phase 4.5. By cause: external API shape or behaviour assumed rather than recorded 8 (23, 24, 27, 28, 29, 35, 39, 41 = 38 %), NAS performance or database size 7 (22, 25, 26, 31, 32, 34, 36 = 33 %), scope surprise 2 (38, 40), deploy plumbing 2 (21, 37), logic 2 (30, 33). The DDL lock race broke a deploy three times (fixes 13, 21, 37: journal 33, 66, 110). Every full deploy costs a cold-cache storm (loops 90-336 s, journal 109-110) on an executor already over its 7.5 s p95 ceiling, so week-1 data carries the cost of the churn.

Together these cover 13-18 of the 21 escapes.
corrections: Of the 21 carried fixes 21-41, 20 were first found on the NAS (fixes 21, 30, 31, 37 at a deploy step; 22-29, 32, 34-36, 38-41 by post-deploy verify — roadmap.md:341-361, each row naming its site) and fix 33 was found by the phase 5 T11 task review (roadmap.md:353, "ledger", no journal number) after its code was already live from the phase 4.5 deploy f851128 — verified: `iso = now.isocalendar()` at f851128:harness/settlement/report_wtd.py:67 and f851128:harness/dashboard/snapshots/ticket.py:232. So 21 of 21 were in production before anyone caught them; none was caught by pre-deploy test or review. By cause: external API shape or behaviour assumed rather than recorded 7-10 depending on where fixes 38/40/41 are placed (23, 24, 27, 28, 29, 35, 39 firmly; journal 110 calls 38 the same class — "the venue's communications channel is not the sporadic combo trickle the addendum assumed" — while 41 is really our own input-size estimate: WORST_CASE_INPUT_TOKENS 30,000 vs 46,528 observed, MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS 1,024); NAS performance or database size 7 (22, 25, 26, 31, 32, 34, 36 = 33 %); deploy plumbing 2 (21, 37); logic 2-3 (30, 33, and arguably 41). Either way the two environment classes account for 14-15 of 21 (67-71 %), and roadmap.md:108-109's stated policy — "Each feature is coded and tested against recorded shapes" — sits directly above a Secrets table naming the Kalshi demo key (the smoke that produced 24, 27, 28, 29) and secrets/anthropic_api_key (39, 41), so it is the right policy to measure against and it was not followed for the Kalshi V2 write path or the Anthropic request path. The DDL lock problem broke a deploy three times (fixes 13, 21, 37: journal 33, 66, 110) — a deadlock the first time, a lock_timeout the next two, the same family each time. A full deploy on this box costs a cold-cache storm: executor loops 91 s and 129 s (journal 109), 99.9 s (journal 110), 40 s even on an app-only deploy (journal 112), and 171 s at the phase 4.5 deploy with the scheduler on (journal 89), on an executor whose day p95 is 16.2 / 6.2 / 15.2 / 10.0 s (evidence.md D1) against a 7.5 s ceiling (verify.md:117, exec_period_s x 1000 / 2) — though the live heartbeat currently reads 7,112 ms, just under it. The 235-336 s loops belong to the 03:30 pg_dump x RFQ replay (journal 109), not to a deploy, and fix 35 has since addressed that path. Week-1 data carries the cost of this churn.

Of the 21 carried fixes 21-41, 14 (67 %) reached a running production build; 6 did not — fixes 24, 27, 28 and 29 were caught by the demo smoke, a play-money staging gate the roadmap provisions for exactly this purpose (roadmap.md:113-115; journal 68 "prod untouched", 76 "paper never runs the writer", 82 "prod has no row"), and fixes 21 and 37 aborted their deploys with the prior build left running (journal 33 "No data lost"). Fix 33 reached production but produced no wrong output: gate_reports has 0 rows and docs/reports/ is empty, so no report was ever keyed with the UTC week. The carried-fix list is not a valid escape-rate denominator — it is by definition the set found at deploy/verify; measured against total defects found, phase 5 caught roughly 45-50 findings pre-merge (12C+12I pre-flight scan, per-task reviews, 2C/5I/11M final review) against 9 carried fixes, an escape rate near 18 %. The cause taxonomy should be restated: at most 2 of the 8 "external API shape assumed rather than recorded" items are shape assumptions (23, 24); 27 and 28 are venue read-after-write timing that no fixture can capture, 39 is an SDK/API structured-output keyword asymmetry found despite recorded Anthropic fixtures (sdd-ledger:22; journal 110), 41 is a token-budget miscalibration, and 35/38/40 are venue traffic-volume surprises. The roadmap.md:108-110 "recorded shapes" sentence sits under "## Secrets" and governs secret-gated switch-on, not integration testing generally. The deploy-churn consequence does not hold: journal 109 measures the storm as "no order placed or lost ... no spend ... the tape intact", recovery in four loops, all deploys in quiet hours under R4, and daily order placement rose 1,258 → 2,615 → 3,836 across the churn; the 235-336 s loops were the RFQ listener × nightly pg_dump, not a deploy. The binding constraints on week-1 data are the exec_max_open_orders = 150 cap (binding in 41 of 53 hours, evidence.md:968) and the fair_stale/pricing-lateness interaction (7,825 of 7,997 cancels; stale_allowance 220 s on every order; no fair values 01:30-07:30 CT on 09-11, evidence.md:965), the latter an open user decision since 2026-09-09. What stands: the no-op-ALTER root cause was visible in journal 33 but not fixed until fix 37, two deploy failures later — one Important; and the seven NAS-performance findings are a host-capacity fact recorded on day one (R17: "7 GB RAM with ~1 GB available") under a one-environment ruling (R15), correctly escalated to the Mac mini decision (journal 101), not a process failure. Severity: Medium, not Critical — no money, order, or tape loss is recorded against any of the 21.

Severity: major (not critical), question: process, recommendation amended. Of the 21 carried fixes 21-41, 20 were first found on the NAS (21, 30, 31, 37 at a deploy step; the other 16 by post-deploy verify) and only fix 33 by a pre-deploy review; by cause, external API shape or behaviour assumed rather than recorded accounts for 8 (23, 24, 27, 28, 29, 35, 39, 41) and NAS performance or database size for 7 (22, 25, 26, 31, 32, 34, 36), so 71% of escapes fall in two environment classes that the local test suite structurally cannot reach. Major rather than critical because the loop's own verify caught all 21 within hours, the paper ledger and the 3,000-unit bankrolls are intact, no money is at risk, and with no staging environment 'first found on the NAS' is partly by design -- but it is not minor, because the churn cost (executor loops 90-336 s against a 7.5 s p95 ceiling, executor down 05:20-05:24, RFQ listener off twice and the research worker off once on 2026-09-11, journal 109/110) lands inside the week-1 window that the owner evaluates at the Mon 2026-09-14 09:00 CT gate, and because it inverts the Mac mini question: a faster host addresses at most the 7 NAS/db escapes and none of the 8 external-shape ones. Amended recommendation, in value order: (1) EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the drill's restored NAS-sized copy (deploy/backup/drill.sh already exists) required for any bulk-table query or snapshot builder -- covers 7 escapes at near-zero setup cost; (2) run `harness kalshi-smoke --env demo` as a pre-merge gate rather than only post-deploy -- it is what actually found 24, 27, 28 and 29, which no read-only probe can reach; (3) a recorded-fixture requirement for read-only external shapes and for the Anthropic request path (a token count of the rendered view would have shown 46.5k against the 30k worst case, fix 41) -- covers roughly 4 more. Honest combined coverage is ~11-15 of 21, not 13-18. Drop journal 43's 66 min of lost tape from the evidence: that was the planned U3 partition migration, journaled as an accepted cost, not an escape.

corrections: Final reviews catch real Criticals, and they catch the code-internal class; the environment class escapes to production. Verified counts: phase 4 1 Critical / 3 Important (journal 65 at journal.md:879; 2026-09-08-phase4-final-review.md:7 — the first deploy did abort at backup-precheck, journal 66); phase 4.5 4 Critical / 9 Important across two opus lenses (final-review.md:16 "1 Critical, 4 Important, 8 Minor" + :229 "3 Critical, 5 Important, 6 Minor"; journal 87 — session poisoning on a DB-level section failure, envelope error rendered nowhere, Floor's venue tripwire green on failure, five of six sparklines never draw); phase 5 2 Critical / 5 Important / 11 Minor (2026-09-10-phase5-final-review.md:26; C1 harness/research/veto.py:225-227 — the grader matched ids the model never sees, so H9 would have measured nothing; C2 annotator bullets write-only).
